full_judgment:
5. Mrs. Mahmuda Parveen next submits that it has been held in the decision in the case of the Circle Officer, Sutrapur vs Mohammad reported in 43 DLR 84 that in dealing with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act, in the case of the Government, public interest has to be duly considered and various authorities, formalities and complications are involved and, as such, the Government requires a longer time in making its decision and acting on it and if, on behalf of the Government, a reasonable explanation of delay is given, there is no reason why it should not be accepted. 

 9. Mr Humayun Kabir Sikder next submits that the law of limitation enjoins that the Government and the public litigant stand on equal footing and every day's delay is to be explained satisfactorily and as the petitioners have failed to explain away every day's delay in filing the revisional application, the delay of 336 days in filing the same should not be condoned and consequently, the Rule should be discharged. In this connection, Mr Humayun Kabir Sikder adverts to the decision in the case of Abul Quasem vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 6 MLR 73= 6 BLC 259. 

 10. I have heard the submissions of the learned Assistant Attorney-General Mrs. Mahmuda Parveen and the counter-submissions of the learned Advocate Mr Humayun Kabir Sikder and perused the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act filed by the petitioners. 

 11. In order to set the controversy at rest, section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 may be quoted below verbatim: 

 "5. Any appeal or application for a revision or a review of judgment or for leave to appeal or any other application to which this may be made applicable by or under any enactment for the time being in force, may be admitted after the period of limitation prescribed thereof, when the appellant or applicant satisfies the Court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or making the application within such period." 

 14. From the decision in the case of the Chairman, Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha vs Rokeya Begum reported in 6 MLR (AD) 295 referred to by the learned Advocate Mr Humayun Kabir Sikder, it transpires that the petitioner moved the High Court Division with an application under section 115( 1) of the Code of Civil Procedure which was out of time by 1,345 days and since the inordinate delay was not at all explained away, the High Court Division summarily rejected it as being barred by limitation and thereafter the petitioner presented a Civil Petition For Leave. To Appeal to the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division did not interfere with the order of the High Court Division on the ground that any indulgence regardless of the settled principles of law and practice will only give a premium to negligence or want of due diligence in public office which is not desirable. 

 15. In the decision in the case of Abul Quasem vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 6 MLR 73 =6 BLC 259 adverted to by the learned Advocate Mr Humayun Kabir Sikder, it has been held that the law of limitation enjoins that the Government and public litigants stand on equal footing and every day's delay is to be explained satisfactorily; but it is not always an absolute rule and the nature of explanation depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. It has been further held in the said decision that though the Government cannot claim any special privilege, yet some consideration may be given in view of the Government functionaries working in a time consuming process while condoning delay in an appropriate case. 

 16. The upshot of the above discussions is that although the Government is not entitled to any special privilege in the matter of condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act, yet some consideration may be given thereto depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case where the Government appears as a litigant. This is because the Government machinery moves at a snail's pace and the Government functionaries work in a time-consuming process. However, it is true that each day's delay has not been explained away in the application for condonation of delay in the present case before us. But this is not an absolute rule. In such a landscape, no strait-jacket formula can be laid down in this regard. What I am driving at boils down to this condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case.
